models.title: Singer-Terhaar blended risk premium for partially integrated markets
models.summary: Asset risk premium as the integration-weighted average of the fully-integrated global-CAPM premium and the fully-segmented local premium.

relationship.locator: PDF: LM2 Forecasting Equity Returns, printed p. 88 (PDF p. 98), Eq. 6; worked example printed p. 89 (PDF p. 99)
relationship.translation_notes: Source expresses rates as percentages; record uses decimal form (unit 1) with no conversion factor inlined. phi is the degree of global integration (1 = fully integrated). Component premiums RPiG (Eq. 4) and RPiS (Eq. 5) are curated as separate companion records. Dimensional check: dimensionless weights times dimensionless premiums, sum is a dimensionless premium.

variables.definition: Degree to which the asset's market is globally integrated, from 0 (fully segmented) to 1 (fully integrated)
variables.context: same asset and global market pair as RPi

variables.definition: Risk premium under full global integration (global-CAPM component, Eq. 4), in decimal form
variables.context: same asset and global market pair as RPi

variables.definition: Risk premium under complete segmentation (asset as its own market, Eq. 5), in decimal form
variables.context: same asset and segmented market as RPi

variables.definition: Final Singer-Terhaar risk premium estimate for asset i, in decimal form; expected return adds the risk-free rate
variables.context: same asset and global market pair as inputs

assumptions: The analyst supplies phi as a judgment about integration (source suggests 0.75–0.90 for developed, 0.50–0.75 for emerging markets as starting points).
Source assumption: pragmatic implementation sets all Sharpe ratios equal to the global Sharpe ratio.
limitations: phi is a judgmental input, not estimated by the model; results are sensitive to it.
A more complex variant allowing within-country asset-class integration (per source footnote 14) is outside this record.

sources.title: Equity Forecasting Models (AnalystPrep CFA Level III study notes)
sources.locator: Singer-Terhaar Model section: ERP_i as degree-of-integration times integrated component plus degree-of-segmentation times segmented component
sources.evidence: Page states the model blends a fully segmented and a fully integrated market with an adjustment for the degree of integration, giving ERP as integration-weighted integrated term plus segmentation-weighted segmented term — the same weighted-average structure as the PDF's Eq. 6.
sources.redistribution: Short original paraphrase and single-formula transcription only; no extended quotation

references.method: Source inputs (3.57% integrated, 5.95% segmented, phi 0.85) in decimals: 0.85·0.0357 + 0.15·0.0595 = 0.03927, matching published 3.93% to stated rounding.
references.provenance: Published result: LM2 worked example, printed p. 89 (PDF p. 99)

references.method: Source inputs (1.05% integrated, 1.75% segmented, phi 0.85) in decimals: 0.85·0.0105 + 0.15·0.0175 = 0.01155, matching published 1.16% to stated rounding.
references.provenance: Published result: LM2 worked example, printed p. 89 (PDF p. 99)

rejection_cases.reason: Integration degree above 1 violates the closed-interval domain (guard phi <= 1); extrapolation beyond full integration needs a different model.
Segmented-market premium is a required input; the blend cannot be formed from the integrated component alone.

models.inverse_notes: Linear in each premium: RPiG = (RPi − (1−phi)·RPiS)/phi requires phi ≠ 0; RPiS = (RPi − phi·RPiG)/(1−phi) requires phi ≠ 1; phi = (RPi − RPiS)/(RPiG − RPiS) requires distinct components. Boundary phi=0 (fully segmented) and phi=1 (fully integrated) are admissible and collapse to one component. Algebraic only; phi remains a judgment, not an estimated quantity.

gaps: Quantity meanings market_integration_degree, integrated_market_risk_premium, segmented_market_risk_premium, blended_risk_premium are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot and require extension.
Companion component records (integrated Eq. 4, segmented Eq. 5) are queued, not yet curated.

models.title: CAPM beta from correlation and volatilities
models.summary: Asset beta as the asset–market correlation times the ratio of asset volatility to market volatility.

relationship.original_equation: βi,M = Cov(Ri, RM) / Var(RM) = ρi,M (σi / σM)
relationship.locator: PDF: LM2 Forecasting Equity Returns, printed p. 88 (PDF p. 98), Eq. 3
relationship.translation_notes: Curated form is the second equality of Eq. 3 (correlation form), which uses only volatilities and correlation rather than covariance/variance moments. sigi and sigm must share the same return-volatility units (unit 1, decimal form). Dimensional check: dimensionless correlation times ratio of two identical volatility dimensions = dimensionless beta.

variables.definition: Correlation between asset i returns and market portfolio returns
variables.context: same asset, market portfolio, and estimation window as beta

variables.definition: Standard deviation of asset i returns, in decimal form
variables.context: same asset and estimation window as beta

variables.definition: Standard deviation of market portfolio returns, in decimal form
variables.context: same market portfolio and estimation window as beta

variables.definition: Asset i sensitivity to the market portfolio (CAPM beta)
variables.context: same asset, market portfolio, and estimation window as inputs
variables.domain: Finite beta; 1 moves with the market, 0 is market-neutral

assumptions: Asset and market volatilities are estimated over the same window and in consistent return units.
Source assumption (CAPM framing): beta measures sensitivity to the stated market portfolio.
limitations: Point estimate conditional on the estimation window; sampling error in correlation and volatilities is not modeled here.
The covariance/variance moment form (first equality of Eq. 3) is an equivalent restatement, not a separate record.

sources.title: CAPM Beta Explained and Formula Examples (AnalystPrep blog)
sources.locator: Beta formulae section: βi = Cov(i,m)/σ²m = ρim × σi/σm, with worked examples
sources.evidence: Page derives beta as covariance over market variance and equivalently as correlation times the asset-to-market volatility ratio, with a worked example (0.6 × 0.18/0.14 = 0.77) confirming the curated form.
sources.redistribution: Short original paraphrase and single-formula transcription only; no extended quotation

references.method: Corroborating source's worked example recomputed: 0.6 × 0.18/0.14 = 0.7714 (source rounds to 0.77).
references.provenance: Published result: AnalystPrep beta article Example 1, with documented rounding

references.method: Perfectly correlated equal volatilities give beta 1 by direct substitution. Independently constructed boundary check.
references.provenance: Independent arithmetic check constructed for this record; no observed market data claimed

rejection_cases.reason: Zero market volatility makes beta undefined (guard sigm > 0); a degenerate constant market needs a different treatment.

models.inverse_notes: rho = beta·sigm/sigi requires sigi ≠ 0; sigi = beta·sigm/rho requires rho ≠ 0; sigm = rho·sigi/beta requires beta ≠ 0. The covariance form β = Cov/Var is an equivalent restatement of the same relationship, not a separate model. Algebraic only; correlation is estimated, not caused, by inversion.

models.title: Building-block fixed-income expected return
models.summary: Required/expected fixed-income return as the short-term default-free rate plus term, credit, and liquidity premiums.

relationship.original_equation: Required return = one-period default-free rate + term premium + credit premium + liquidity premium
relationship.locator: PDF: LM2 Forecasting Fixed Income Returns, printed p. 74 (PDF p. 84); applied in LM2 Solutions, printed p. 129 (PDF p. 139), Q1
relationship.translation_notes: Source states the four components in prose (premiums compensate interest-rate/duration, credit, and illiquidity risk); record formalizes the stated sum. Decimal form (unit 1) with no conversion factor. Dimensional check: sum of four dimensionless rates.

variables.definition: One-period (short-term) default-free rate matching the forecast horizon, in decimal form
variables.context: same fixed-income asset class and forecast horizon as ER

variables.definition: Additional expected return for duration/interest-rate risk, in decimal form
variables.context: same fixed-income asset class and forecast horizon as ER

variables.definition: Additional expected return for bearing default losses beyond expected loss levels, in decimal form
variables.context: same fixed-income asset class and forecast horizon as ER

variables.definition: Additional expected return for illiquidity, in decimal form
variables.context: same fixed-income asset class and forecast horizon as ER

variables.definition: Building-block required/expected return for the fixed-income asset class, in decimal form
variables.context: same fixed-income asset class and forecast horizon as inputs

assumptions: Premiums are stated consistently (same horizon, same compounding) and only the short-term default-free rate is potentially observable; the rest are estimated.
Forecast horizons much longer than the short instrument need the source's maturity-matching adjustment (outside this sum).
limitations: Premiums are embedded in yield spreads but do not equal observed spreads (per source); estimating them is outside this definitional sum.
In extreme cases (e.g. negative policy rates) the source advises normalizing the short rate or raising a premium rather than using the raw observation.

models.title: Net exports equals private saving gap plus government surplus
models.summary: National income accounting identity: net exports (X − M) equals net private saving (S − I) plus the government surplus (T − G).

relationship.locator: PDF: LM1 International Interactions, printed p. 48 (PDF p. 58)
relationship.translation_notes: TS is introduced for the source symbol (T − G) and defined as the government surplus. All amounts are levels in the same domestic currency unit over the same accounting period. Dimensional check: currency − currency + currency = currency. Record uses USD as the single-currency unit label; the identity holds in any single currency.

variables.definition: Domestic private saving (excess of private saving over the stated period)
variables.context: same economy and national-accounts period as NX
variables.domain: Finite saving level; may be any sign per accounts

variables.definition: Domestic private investment spending over the stated period
variables.context: same economy and national-accounts period as NX

variables.definition: Government surplus: tax revenue minus government spending over the stated period; negative when in deficit
variables.context: same economy and national-accounts period as NX
variables.domain: Finite surplus level; negative admits the deficit case

variables.definition: Net exports: exports minus imports over the stated period
variables.context: same economy and national-accounts period as inputs
variables.domain: Finite net export level; negative admits the trade-deficit case

assumptions: Standard national income accounting with consistent period, economy, and a single currency unit throughout.
Net exports is the dominant current-account component in the source's framing; the identity itself is exact by construction.
limitations: Accounting identity only: it constrains joint movements but does not establish causation between saving, fiscal balance, and trade.
Reversing all signs gives the capital-account mirror statement (per source); that restatement is not a separate record.

sources.title: Principles of Macroeconomics, Ch. 13.2 Saving and Investment in the National Income Accounts (SUNY open textbook)
sources.version: Open textbook section 13.2, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, accessed 2026-11-04
sources.locator: Section 13.2a identities: S = I + NX, S − I = NX; (Y − T − C) + (T − G) = I decomposition into private and public saving
sources.evidence: Section derives S − I = NX (trade balance) and splits national saving into private (Y − T − C) and public (T − G) saving — the same decomposition the PDF writes as (S − I) + (T − G).
sources.redistribution: Short original paraphrase and single-formula transcription only; no extended quotation

references.method: Direct substitution: (1200 − 1150) + 50 = 100. Independently constructed arithmetic check in a single currency unit.
references.provenance: Independent arithmetic check constructed for this record; no observed national-accounts data claimed

references.method: Balanced private saving/investment with balanced budget gives zero net exports by substitution.
references.provenance: Definitional boundary check; not an empirical validation

rejection_cases.reason: Government surplus is a required term of the identity; private saving gap alone cannot determine net exports.

models.inverse_notes: Linear in each term: S = NX + I − TS; I = S + TS − NX; TS = NX − S + I. No singularities. Algebraic only; the identity does not identify which component adjusts when another changes.

gaps: Quantity meanings private_saving, private_investment, government_surplus, net_exports are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot and require extension.
USD is used as the single domestic-currency unit label; cross-currency use would need an explicit exchange-rate model per the no-implicit-conversion rule.
